hits.name: Arpit Bhayani
hits.text:
Somewhere in your company, there is probably a service running in production that nobody has actually read. It handles real traffic. One person vibe-coded it, watched it pass a few manual checks, and shipped it.

That person is the only one who has any "feel" for how it behaves. Now imagine they leave. What happens when something goes wrong... Most of the reasoning, checks, and flows existed in some Claude session that nobody saved, and in the head of someone who is now gone.

To be fair, this is not a new problem. We all kind of have been in similar situations earlier as well, but what changes with vibe-coding is how fast you can create one, and how thin the understanding is even for the author. "I wrote it, so I know it" is weaker when you did not really write it.

Here are some ways of fixing it that I am trying out -

- Review, rather than understand, generated code like any other code. If nobody on the team can explain it, it should not go to production.

- The language and infra should be familiar; do not pick a language just because you could

- Keep the intent somewhere durable. A short note on what the service is for and why the non-obvious decisions were made is enough - best place: code comments.

- Make sure at least two people can operate and debug every production service.

Move fast, yes. Use LLM to write and ship, yes. Just make sure you + 1 understand what you shipped.

Hope this helps.

Own your intelligence stack, folks!

I will never get tired of saying this. Your business's very existence is at play here. 

But you don't have to do this all at once if you can't afford it. I mean, open models are still very expensive to run and tune. 

If you want to start somewhere, I suggest the harness. Build your evals and quickly move down the stack. 

The great part about building your own harness is that it gives you optionality, unlocks capabilities, and helps you measure where else in the intelligence stack you need to invest next. 

So while open-source was an alternative in the old era, today it is how you survive and thrive in the age of intelligence.

hits.name: Arpit Bhayani
hits.text:
pro tip: structure the codebase before you ask your agents to write tests.

This one "step" has improved the quality of tests more than any prompt tweak I have tried. When files and directories follow a clear convention, the model knows where each piece of logic lives, what its dependencies are, and what a test for it should look like.

This way, it can write focused tests for each layer, mock the right boundaries (if relevant), and cover more branches in the first go.

If you let it go loose and just say "write tests", it only sees whatever code you point it at. It tends to cover the obvious happy paths and miss the rest.

Now flip it. If the code is already spaghetti, with business logic mixed into handlers, weird global state, and functions doing five things, the LLM has nothing clean to hold on to. It either writes brittle tests or tests that pass without actually verifying much.

So, in a gist - messy structure, messy tests.

The order matters - fix the structure first, or ask the LLM to follow one from the start, and only then ask it to write tests.

hits.original_en:
pro tip: structure the codebase before you ask your agents to write tests.

This one "step" has improved the quality of tests more than any prompt tweak I have tried. When files and directories follow a clear convention, the model knows where each piece of logic lives, what its dependencies are, and what a test for it should look like.

This way, it can write focused tests for each layer, mock the right boundaries (if relevant), and cover more branches in the first go.

If you let it go loose and just say "write tests", it only sees whatever code you point it at. It tends to cover the obvious happy paths and miss the rest.

Now flip it. If the code is already spaghetti, with business logic mixed into handlers, weird global state, and functions doing five things, the LLM has nothing clean to hold on to. It either writes brittle tests or tests that pass without actually verifying much.

So, in a gist - messy structure, messy tests.

The order matters - fix the structure first, or ask the LLM to follow one from the start, and only then ask it to write tests.

Good structure was always good for humans. Turns out, it helps the machine too - a trend we have been seeing for quite some time now :)

Hope this helps.

hits.name: elvis
hits.text:
Nice paper on CoT controllability.

They find that chain-of-thought monitoring depends partly on models being unable to control what they write in their reasoning.

They traced much of that limit to the first few tokens after the opening thinking tag. Entropy collapses there, and the model falls into a few common openings.

Small changes at that point restore a lot of control. Prefilling a single token raised controllability substantially. Banning frequent opening tokens and adding in-context examples raised average compliance by 34 to 41 points across models.

These interventions mostly restore control over adding or restyling information. Control over leaving information out responded less consistently.

The two kinds behave like separate capabilities. Across models, scores correlate within each group and mostly negatively between groups.

https://t.co/PdxT5o9Nk9

Chat with Paper: https://t.co/sjJ20A50J8

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
